entries.3b4df58a1a308704f506a83c597eb135bc1760e2: <div sID="gen7707" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="1Chr.9" sID="1Chr.9"/> <div eID="gen7707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7708" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7709" type="x-p"/> This chapter intimates to us that one end of recording all these genealogies was to direct the Jews, now that they had returned out of captivity, with whom to incorporate and where to reside; for here we have an account of those who first took possession of Jerusalem after their return from Babylon, and began the rebuilding of it upon the old foundation. I. The Israelites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2-1Chr.9.9">ver. 2-9</reference>. II. The priests, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10-1Chr.9.13">ver. 10-13</reference>. III. The Levites and other Nethinim, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.14-1Chr.9.26">ver. 14-26</reference>. IV. Here is the particular charge of some of the priests and Levites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.27-1Chr.9.34">ver. 27-34</reference>. V. A repetition of the genealogy of king Saul, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35-1Chr.9.44">ver. 35-44</reference>.
entries.7f5e63c27debcd596c6cf23d14bddc735965e45e: <div eID="gen7709" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7708" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 700.)</title> <div sID="gen7710" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they <hi type="italic">were</hi> written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, <hi type="italic">who</hi> were carried away to Babylon for their transgression. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now the first inhabitants that <hi type="italic">dwelt</hi> in their possessions in their cities <hi type="italic">were,</hi> the Israelites, the priests, Levites, and the Nethinims. <hi type="super">3</hi> And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh; <hi type="super">4</hi> Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah. <hi type="super">5</hi> And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. <hi type="super">6</hi> And of the sons of Zerah; Jeuel, and their brethren, six hundred and ninety. <hi type="super">7</hi> And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah, <hi type="super">8</hi> And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephathiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah; <hi type="super">9</hi> And their brethren, according to their generations, nine hundred and fifty and six. All these men <hi type="italic">were</hi> chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers. <hi type="super">10</hi> And of the priests; Jedaiah, and Jehoiarib, and Jachin, <hi type="super">11</hi> And Azariah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of the house of God; <hi type="super">12</hi> And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer; <hi type="super">13</hi> And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God. <div eID="gen7710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7711" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">The first verse</reference> looks back upon the foregoing genealogies, and tells us they were gathered out of <hi type="italic">the books of the kings of Israel and Judah,</hi> not that which we have in the canon of scripture, but another civil record, which was authentic, as the king's books with us. Mentioning Israel and Judah, the historian takes notice of their being <hi type="italic">carried away to Babylon for their transgression.</hi> Let that judgment never be forgotten, but ever be remembered, for warning to posterity to take heed of those sins that brought it upon them. Whenever we speak of any calamity that has befallen us, it is good to add this, "it was for my transgression," that God may be justified and clear when he judges. Then follows an account of the first inhabitants, after their return from captivity, that dwelt in their cities, especially in Jerusalem. 1. The Israelites. That general name is used (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2">v. 2</reference>) because with those of Judah and Benjamin there were many of Ephraim and Manasseh, and the other ten tribes (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">v. 3</reference>), such as had escaped to Judah when the body of the ten tribes were carried captive or returned to Judah upon the revolutions in Assyria, and so went into captivity with them, or met them when they were in Babylon, associated with them, and so shared in the benefit of their enlargement. It was foretold that the <hi type="italic">children of Judah and of Israel</hi> should be <hi type="italic">gathered together and come up out of the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Hos. i. 11</reference>), and that they should be one nation again, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.22">Ezek. xxxvii. 22</reference>. Trouble drives those together that have been at variance; and the pieces of metal that had been separated will run together again when melted in the same crucible. Many both of Judah and Israel staid behind in captivity; but some of both, whose spirit God stirred up, enquired the way to Zion again. Divers are here named, and many more numbered, who were <hi type="italic">chief of the fathers</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.9">v. 9</reference>), who ought to be remembered with honour, as Israelites indeed. 2. The priests, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10">v. 10</reference>. It was their praise that they came with the first. Who should lead in a good work if the priests, the Lord's ministers, do not? It was the people's praise that they would not come without them; for who but the priests should keep knowledge? Who but the priests should bless them in the name of the Lord? (1.) It is said of one of them that he was <hi type="italic">the ruler of the house of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.11">v. 11</reference>) not the chief ruler, for Joshua was then the high priest, but the sagan, and the next under him, his deputy, who perhaps applied more diligently to the business than the high priest himself. In the house of God it is requisite that there be rulers, not to make new laws, but to take care that the laws of God be duly observed by priests as well as people. (2.) It is said of many of them that they were <hi type="italic">very able men for the service of the house of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.13">v. 13</reference>. In the house of God there is service to be done, constant service; and it is well for the church when those are employed in that service who are qualified for it, <hi type="italic">able ministers of the New Testament,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2 Cor. iii. 6</reference>. The service of the temple was such as required at all times, especially in this critical juncture, when they had newly come out of Babylon, great courage and vigour of mind, as well as strength of body; and therefore they are praised as <hi type="italic">mighty men of valour.</hi>
entries.5f54fd4724194f1f778dbcb74cb63be1d2e9d629: <div eID="gen7711" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies; the Employment of the Priests. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1400.)</title> <div sID="gen7712" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari; <hi type="super">15</hi> And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph; <hi type="super">16</hi> And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the porters <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum <hi type="italic">was</hi> the chief; <hi type="super">18</hi> Who hitherto <hi type="italic">waited</hi> in the king's gate eastward: they <hi type="italic">were</hi> porters in the companies of the children of Levi. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, <hi type="italic">were</hi> over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, <hi type="italic">being</hi> over the host of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">were</hi> keepers of the entry. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the ruler over them in time past, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">was</hi> with him. <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah <hi type="italic">was</hi> porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">22</hi> All these <hi type="italic">which were</hi> chosen to be porters in the gates <hi type="italic">were</hi> two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office. <hi type="super">23</hi> So they and their children <hi type="italic">had</hi> the oversight of the gates of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> the house of the tabernacle, by wards. <hi type="super">24</hi> In four quarters were the porters, toward the east, west, north, and south. <hi type="super">25</hi> And their brethren, <hi type="italic">which were</hi> in their villages, <hi type="italic">were</hi> to come after seven days from time to time with them. <hi type="super">26</hi> For these Levites, the four chief porters, were in <hi type="italic">their</hi> set office, and were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of God. <hi type="super">27</hi> And they lodged round about the house of God, because the charge <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon them, and the opening thereof every morning <hi type="italic">pertained</hi> to them. <hi type="super">28</hi> And <hi type="italic">certain</hi> of them had the charge of the ministering vessels, that they should bring them in and out by tale. <hi type="super">29</hi> <hi type="italic">Some</hi> of them also <hi type="italic">were</hi> appointed to oversee the vessels, and all the instruments of the sanctuary, and the fine flour, and the wine, and the oil, and the frankincense, and the spices. <hi type="super">30</hi> And <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the sons of the priests made the ointment of the spices. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Mattithiah, <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the Levites, who <hi type="italic">was</hi> the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans. <hi type="super">32</hi> And <hi type="italic">other</hi> of their brethren, of the sons of the Kohathites, <hi type="italic">were</hi> over the showbread, to prepare <hi type="italic">it</hi> every sabbath. <hi type="super">33</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, <hi type="italic">who remaining</hi> in the chambers <hi type="italic">were</hi> free: for they were employed in <hi type="italic">that</hi> work day and night. <hi type="super">34</hi> These chief fathers of the Levites <hi type="italic">were</hi> chief throughout their generations; these dwelt at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen7712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7713" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of the good posture which the affairs of religion were put into immediately upon the return of the people out of Babylon. They had smarted for their former neglect of ordinances and under the late want of ordinances. Both these considerations made them very zealous and forward in setting up the worship of God among them; so they began their worship of God at the right end. Instances hereof we have here. <div eID="gen7713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7714" type="x-p"/> I. Before the house of the Lord was built they had the house of the tabernacle, a plain and movable tent, which they made use of in the mean time. Those that cannot yet reach to have a temple must not be without a tabernacle, but be thankful for that and make the best of it. Never let God's work be left undone for want of a place to do it in. <div eID="gen7714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7715" type="x-p"/> II. In allotting to the priests and Levites their respective employments, they had an eye to the model that was drawn up by David, and Samuel the seer, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">v. 22</reference>. Samuel, in his time, had drawn the scheme of it, and laid the foundation, though the ark was then in obscurity, and David afterwards finished it, and both acted by immediate direction from God. Or David, as soon as he was anointed had this matter in his mind and consulted Samuel about it, though he was then in his troubles, and the plan was formed in concert between them. This perhaps had been little regarded for many ages; but now, after a long interruption, it was revived. In dividing the work, they observed these ancient land-marks. <div eID="gen7715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7716" type="x-p"/> III. The most of them dwelt at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.34">v. 34</reference>), yet there were some that dwelt in the villages (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.16">v. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">22</reference>), because, it may be, there was not yet room for them in Jerusalem. However they were employed in the service of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">They were to come after seven days from time to time.</hi> They had their week's attendance in their turns. <div eID="gen7716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7717" type="x-p"/> IV. Many of the Levites were employed as porters at the gates of the house of God, four chief porters (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.26">v. 26</reference>), and, under them, others, to the number of 212, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">v. 22</reference>. They had the oversight of the gates (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.23">v. 23</reference>), were keepers of the <hi type="italic">thresholds,</hi> as in the margin (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.19">v. 19</reference>), and keepers of the entry. This seemed a mean office; and yet David would rather have it than <hi type="italic">dwell in the tents of wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Ps. lxxxiv. 10</reference>. Their office was, 1. To open the doors of God's house every morning (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.27">v. 27</reference>) and shut them at night. 2. To keep off the unclean, and hinder those from thrusting in that were forbidden by the law. 3. To direct and introduce into the courts of the Lord those that came thither to worship, and to show them where to go and what to do, that they might not incur punishment. This required care, and diligence, and constant attendance. Ministers have work to do of this kind. <div eID="gen7717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7718" type="x-p"/> V. Here is one Phinehas, a son of Eleazar, that is said to be a <hi type="italic">ruler over them in time past</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.20">v. 20</reference>), not the famous high priest of that name, but (as is supposed) an eminent Levite, of whom it is here said that <hi type="italic">the Lord was with him,</hi> or (as the Chaldee reads it) <hi type="italic">the Word of the Lord was his helper</hi>—the eternal Word, who is <hi type="italic">Jehovah, the mighty one on whom help is laid.</hi> <div eID="gen7718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7719" type="x-p"/> VI. It is said of some of them that, because the charge was upon them, <hi type="italic">they lodged round about the house of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.27">v. 27</reference>. It is good for ministers to be near their work, that they may give themselves wholly to it. The Levites pitched about the tabernacle when they marched through the wilderness. Then they were porters in one sense, bearing the burdens of the sanctuary, now porters in another sense, attending the gates and the doors—in both instances keeping the charge of the sanctuary. <div eID="gen7719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7720" type="x-p"/> VII. Every one knew his charge. Some were entrusted with the plate, the ministering vessels, to bring them in and out by tale, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.28">v. 28</reference>. Others were appointed to prepare the fine flour, wine, oil, &c., <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.29">v. 29</reference>. Others, that were priests, made up the holy anointing oil, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.30">v. 30</reference>. Others took care of the meat-offerings, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.31">v. 31</reference>. Others of the show-bread, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.32">v. 32</reference>. As in other great houses, so in God's house, the work is likely to be done well when every one knows the duty of his place and makes a business of it. God is the God of order: but that which is every body's work will be nobody's work. <div eID="gen7720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7721" type="x-p"/> VIII. The singers <hi type="italic">were employed in that work day and night,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.33">v. 33</reference>. They were the <hi type="italic">chief fathers of the Levites</hi> that made a business of it, not mean singing-men, that made a trade of it. They remained in the chambers of the temple, that they might closely and constantly attend it, and were therefore excused from all other services. It should seem, some companies were continually singing, at least at stated hours, both day and night. Thus was God continually praised, as it is fit he should be who is continually doing good. Thus devout people might, at any hour, have assistance in their devotion. Thus was the temple a figure of the heavenly one, where they <hi type="italic">rest not day nor night</hi> from praising God, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Blessed are those that dwell in thy house; they will be still praising thee.</hi>
entries.bdef44f7409e93c9cb3cca0a8c0b4d11c05d48e6: <div eID="gen7721" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1400.)</title> <div sID="gen7722" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And in Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jehiel, whose wife's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Maachah: <hi type="super">36</hi> And his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Ner, and Nadab, <hi type="super">37</hi> And Gedor, and Ahio, and Zechariah, and Mikloth. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Mikloth begat Shimeam. And they also dwelt with their brethren at Jerusalem, over against their brethren. <hi type="super">39</hi> And Ner begat Kish; and Kish begat Saul; and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal. <hi type="super">40</hi> And the son of Jonathan <hi type="italic">was</hi> Merib-baal: and Merib-baal begat <reference osisRef="Mic.41">Micah.   41</reference> And the sons of Micah <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Pithon, and Melech, and Tahrea, <hi type="italic">and Ahaz.</hi> <hi type="super">42</hi> And Ahaz begat Jarah; and Jarah begat Alemeth, and Azmaveth, and Zimri; and Zimri begat Moza; <hi type="super">43</hi> And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. <hi type="super">44</hi> And Azel had six sons, whose names <hi type="italic">are</hi> these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan: these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the sons of Azel. <div eID="gen7722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7723" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35-1Chr.9.44">These verses</reference> are the very same with <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29-1Chr.8.38">ch. viii. 29-38</reference>, giving an account of the ancestors of Saul and the posterity of Jonathan. <hi type="italic">There</hi> it is the conclusion of the genealogy of Benjamin; <hi type="italic">here</hi> it is an introduction to the story of Saul. We take the repetition as we find it; but if we admit that there are in the originals, especially in these books, some errors of the transcribers, I should be tempted to think this repetition arose from a blunder. Some one, in copying out these genealogies, having written those words, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.34">v. 34</reference> (<hi type="italic">These dwelt in Jerusalem</hi>), cast his eye on the same words, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.28">ch. viii. 28</reference>. (<hi type="italic">These dwelt in Jerusalem</hi>), and so went on with what followed there, instead of going on with what followed here; and, when he perceived his mistake, was loth to make a blot in his book, and so let it stand. We have a rule in our law, <hi type="italic">Redundans non nocet</hi>—<hi type="italic">Redundancies do no harm.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Chr.9"/> <div eID="gen7723" type="x-p"/>

entries.b27e3a1f8c64d0939e1dfe0417655d7c28b215e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3711"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <div sID="gen5314" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1-1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:1-26</reference>. Original Registers of Israel and Judah's Genealogies.<div eID="gen5314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3711"/><hi type="bold">1. all Israel were reckoned by genealogies--</hi>From the beginning of the Hebrew nation, public records were kept, containing a registration of the name of every individual, as well as the tribe and family to which he belonged. "The book of the kings of Israel and Judah" does not refer to the two canonical books that are known in Scripture by that name, but to authenticated copies of those registers, placed under the official care of the sovereigns; and as a great number of the Israelites (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference>) took refuge in Judah during the invasion of Shalmaneser, they carried the public records along with them. The genealogies given in the preceding chapters were drawn from the public records in the archives both of Israel and Judah; and those given in this chapter relate to the period subsequent to the restoration; whence it appears (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.17-1Chr.3.24">1Ch 3:17-24</reference>) that the genealogical registers were kept during the captivity in Babylon. These genealogical tables, then, are of the highest authority for truth and correctness, the earlier portion being extracted from the authenticated records of the nation; and as to those which belong to the time of the captivity, they were drawn up by a contemporary writer, who, besides enjoying the best sources of information, and being of the strictest integrity, was guided and preserved from all error by divine inspiration. <div eID="gen5315" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2a2a21fe91d5191a5abca3e27a989bed8c16889: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3712"/><div sID="gen5316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3712"/><hi type="bold">2. the first inhabitants that dwelt in their possessions--</hi>This chapter relates wholly to the first returned exiles. Almost all the names recur in Nehemiah (<reference osisRef="Neh.11.1-Neh.11.36">Ne 11:1-36</reference>), although there are differences which will be explained there. The same division of the people into four classes was continued after, as before the captivity; namely, the priests, Levites, natives, who now were called by the common name of Israelites, and the Nethinims (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.27">Jos 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.43">Ezr 2:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.20">8:20</reference>). When the historian speaks of "the first inhabitants that dwelt in their possessions," he implies that there were others who afterwards returned and settled in possessions not occupied by the first. Accordingly, we read of a great number returning successively under Ezra, Nehemiah, and at a later period. And some of those who returned to the ancient inheritance of their fathers, had lived before the time of the captivity (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.4">Hag 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen5316" type="x-p"/>
entries.96eb6891cbcdadf5ce19006984b2616eaea1f7f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3713"/><div sID="gen5317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3713"/><hi type="bold">18. the king's gate--</hi>The king had a gate from his palace into the temple (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.18">2Ki 16:18</reference>), which doubtless was kept constantly closed except for the monarch's use; and although there was no king in Israel on the return from the captivity, yet the old ceremonial was kept up, probably in the hope that the scepter would, ere long, be restored to the house of David. It is an honor by which Eastern kings are distinguished, to have a gate exclusively devoted to their own special use, and which is kept constantly closed, except when he goes out or returns (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.2">Eze 44:2</reference>). There being no king then in Israel, this gate would be always shut. <chapter eID="1Chr.9"/>

entries.0c06e5aea448deaa2fb806b9f331bf5918a1f3a5: <div eID="gen13540" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13541" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13541" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13543" type="x-p"/> All Israel reckoned by genealogies, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">1Chr 9:1</reference>. The first inhabitants of Jerusalem, after their return from their captivity, who were chiefs of the fathers, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2-1Chr.9.9">1Chr 9:2-9</reference>. Of the priests, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10-1Chr.9.13">1Chr 9:10-13</reference>; Levites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.14-1Chr.9.16">1Chr 9:14-16</reference>; porters, their work, lodgings, etc., <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17-1Chr.9.29">1Chr 9:17-29</reference>; other officers, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.30-1Chr.9.32">1Chr 9:30-32</reference>; the singers, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.33">1Chr 9:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.34">1Chr 9:34</reference>. A repetition of the genealogy of Saul and his sons, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35-1Chr.9.44">1Chr 9:35-44</reference>. <div eID="gen13543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13544" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> Were reckoned by genealogies - Jarchi considers these as the words of Ezra, the compiler of the book; as if he had said: I have given the genealogies of the Israelites as I have found them in a book which was carried into Babylon, when the people were carried thither for their transgressions; and this book which I found is that which I have transcribed in the preceding chapters.
entries.355167d06a30e83555b126af76f4bef28d4e6d65: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> Now the first inhabitants - This is spoken of those who returned from the Babylonish captivity, and of the time in which they returned; for it is insinuated here that other persons afterwards settled at Jerusalem, though these mentioned here were the first on the return from the captivity. Properly speaking, the divisions mentioned in this verse constituted the whole of the Israelitish people, who were, ever since the days of Joshua, divided into the four following classes: <div eID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> 1. The priests. <div eID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13548" type="x-p"/> 2. The Levites. <div eID="gen13548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13549" type="x-p"/> 3. The common people, or simple Israelites. <div eID="gen13549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13550" type="x-p"/> 4. The Nethinim, or slaves of the temple, the remains of the Gibeonites, who, having deceived Joshua, were condemned to this service <reference osisRef="Jos.9.21">Jos 9:21</reference>, etc. In David's time it is probable that other conquered people were added, as the successors of the Gibeonites were not sufficient to perform all the drudgery of the temple service.
entries.908dc6a2743019247ab8dedba606677da695a432: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13551" type="x-p"/> And in Jerusalem dwelt - Several of the tribes of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, took advantage of the proclamation of Cyrus to return to Jerusalem, and so mingled with the Israelites, and those to whom Jerusalem had previously appertained; and this was necessary in order to provide a sufficient population for so large a city.
entries.3bca8d1f94b0147cd19c5140b725294f432f8f18: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen13551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13552" type="x-p"/> Uthai the son of Ammihud - The list here is nearly the same with those found in Ezra and Nehemiah, and contains those who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel; but the list in Nehemiah is more ample, probably because it contains those who came afterwards. The object of the sacred writer here was to give the list of those who came first. Now the first inhabitants, etc.
entries.e50b91044fa7776cc6329a59bd319985048ce80c: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen13552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13553" type="x-p"/> The ruler of the house of God - The high priest at this time was Jeshua the son of Jozadak, (<reference osisRef="Ezr.3.8">Ezr 3:8</reference>), and Seraiah, (<reference osisRef="Neh.11.11">Neh 11:11</reference>), called here Azariah, was the ruler of the house; the person next in authority to the high priest, and who probably had the guard of the temple and command of the priests, Levites, etc. It is likely that the person here was the same as is called the second priest, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2Kgs 25:18</reference> (note), who was the sagan or high priest's deputy. See the note there.
entries.81fbfa6961c800432eb367a51e0e2454f4706c35: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen13553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> And their brethren - What a prodigious number of ecclesiastics to perform the Divine service of one temple! no less than one thousand seven hundred and eighty able-bodied men! and this number is reckoned independently of the two hundred and twelve porters who served at the gates of the house of the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">1Chr 9:22</reference>.
entries.9c6ad485cd880a4d0056034a86f4c7489d878cbc: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> The king's gate - That by which the kings of Judah went to the temple; see on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.18">2Kgs 16:18</reference> (note).
entries.0efd165b195e878dd4c108861478691360766443: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> Keepers of the entry - Whose business it was to suffer no person to come to the tabernacle but the priests, during the performance of the sacred service; see Jarchi.
entries.025c9352e1e21a40b1dbd864cf2b56b9fbc882df: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13557" type="x-p"/> And Phinehas - The Targum says, "And Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, was ruler over them from ancient times, from the day in which the tabernacle was set up in the wilderness; and the Word of the Lord was his assistant."
entries.b788cead6d1c1c1725373c047fe74a40032f39ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen13557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13558" type="x-p"/> The sons of the priests made the ointment - Only the priests were permitted to make this ointment; all others were forbidden to do it on pain of death; see <reference osisRef="Exo.30.34-Exo.30.38">Exo 30:34-38</reference> (note), and the notes there.
entries.9f4a57850a823f389a654944f4504b6bdbdde966: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen13558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13559" type="x-p"/> Whose wife's name was Maachah - Here our translators have departed from the original, for the word is אחתו achotho, his Sister; but the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee, have Wife; to which may be added <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29">1Chr 8:29</reference>, the parallel place. Almost all the early editions, as well as the MS. editions, have the same reading. Of all the Polyglots the Complutensian alone has אשתו ishto, his Wife. His wife is the reading also of Vatablus's Polyglot, but in the margin he observes that other copies have his sister. There is most certainly a fault somewhere, for Maachah could not be both the sister and wife of Jehiel. Whether, therefore, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29">1Chr 8:29</reference> has been altered from this, or this altered from that, who can tell? A single letter makes the whole difference: if the word be written with ח cheth, it is Sister; if with ש shin, it is Wife. The latter is most probably the true reading. It is so in three very ancient MSS. in my own possession.
entries.ed9c3e4d68ee713eb61491207f84769ebb6cca05: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen13559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13560" type="x-p"/> And Ahaz - This is added by our translators from <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.35">1Chr 8:35</reference>, but such liberties should only be taken in a note; for although the words are now sufficiently distinguished from the text by being printed in Italics, yet it is too much to expect that every editor of a Bible will attend to such distinctions, and in process of time the words will be found incorporated with the text. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35">1Chr 9:35</reference>, and the following verses, are a repetition of what we find in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29-1Chr.8.38">1Chr 8:29-38</reference> (note), where see the notes.  <chapter eID="1Chr.9"/> <div eID="gen13560" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b5a5a8d77dbd8a6177a072380fd55f7ec789033: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1-1Chr.9.2">1Ch 9:1-2</reference> “And all the Israelites were registered; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel, and Judah was led away to Babylon for her transgressions.” The lxx and Vulg. have erroneously connected ויהוּדה with the preceding words, and render, “in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah,” and then have translated the following words וגו הגלוּ arbitrarily. Not less incorrect is Bertheau’s opinion, that Israel here denotes only the tribes of the northern kingdom, because Israel is contrasted with Judah, and kings of Israel are spoken of, for both reasons are quite worthless. “The book of the kings of Israel” is cited in <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.34">2Ch 20:34</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.18">2Ch 33:18</reference>), and is declared by Bertheau himself to be identical with the historical work cited as the “book of the kings of Israel and Judah” (<reference osisRef="2Chr.27.7">2Ch 27:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.27">2Ch 35:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.8">2Ch 36:8</reference>), or as the “book of the kings of Judah and Israel” (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11">2Ch 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.26">2Ch 25:26</reference>, and elsewhere). How then can it be inferred from the shortened title, “book of the kings of Israel,” that kings of the northern kingdom are spoken of? Then, as to the contrast between Israel and Judah, it might, when looked at by itself, be adduced in favour of taking the name in its narrower sense; but when we consider the grouping together in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10">1Ch 9:10</reference> of “Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the Nethinim,” we see clearly that Israel in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2">1Ch 9:2</reference> incontrovertibly denotes the whole Israel of the twelve tribes. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">1Ch 9:1</reference>, Israel is used in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2">1Ch 9:2</reference>; and the contrast between Israel and Judah, therefore, is analogous to the contrast “Judah and Jerusalem,” i.e., Israel is a designation of the whole covenant people, Judah that of one section of it. The position of our verse also at the end of the genealogies of all the tribes of Israel, and not merely of the ten tribes of the northern kingdom, requires that the name Israel should be understood to denote the whole covenant people. That <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">1Ch 9:1</reference> forms the transition from the genealogies to the enumeration of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and so is properly the conclusion of the genealogies in 1 Chron 2-8, is so manifest that Bertheau cannot adduce a single tenable ground for his assertion to the contrary, that “the verse forms clearly quite a new beginning.” For the assertion, “We recognise in it a short introduction to the historical statements regarding the tribe of Judah or the Israelites after the exile,” cannot be adduced in support of his view, since it not only contradicts his former assertion that Israel here denotes the northern kingdom, but is also irreconcilable with the words of the verse.<note placement="foot">Bertheau’s further remark, “1Ch 9:1 cannot have been written by our historian, because he did not consider it sufficient to refer his readers to the work he quotes from, but thought himself bound to communicate genealogical registers of the tribes of the northern kingdom (1 Chron 5-7), which he must have extracted from older registers prepared in the time of the kings (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.1">1Ch 6:1</reference>), perhaps even out of the work here named,” is quite incomprehensible by me. Notwithstanding repeated consideration of it clause by clause, I have not succeeded in comprehending the logic of this argument.</note> <div eID="gen5665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5666" type="x-p"/> The statement, “Judah was led captive to Babylon for her transgressions,” corresponds to the statement 1Ch 5:25., 1Ch 6:15. But when, after this statement, our writer continues, “And the former inhabitants which (lived) in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the Nethinim; and in Jerusalem there dwelt of the sons of Judah,” etc., the “former inhabitants” can only be those who dwelt in their possessions before Judah was led captive into Babylon. This could hardly be misunderstood by any commentator, if the right interpretation of our passage were not obscured by the similarity of the register of the inhabitants of Jerusalem which follows to that contained in Neh 11, - a similarity which has led some to believe that both registers treat of the post-exilic inhabitants of Jerusalem. Bertheau, e.g., comes to the following decision as to the relation of our register, vv. 2-34, to that in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.3-Neh.11.24">Neh 11:3-24</reference>: “As the result of the comparison, we have found that both registers correspond exactly in their plan, and agree as to all the main points in their contents.” The first point in this result has some foundation; for if we turn our attention only to the enumeration of chiefs dwelling in Jerusalem, then the registers in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.4-1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:4-17</reference> of our chapter and in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.3-Neh.11.19">Neh 11:3-19</reference> are identical in plan. But if we consider the whole of the registers, as found in 1 Chron 9:2-34 and <reference osisRef="Neh.11.3-Neh.11.24">Neh 11:3-24</reference>, we see that they do differ in plan; for in ours, the enumeration of the inhabitants of Jerusalem is introduced by the remark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2">1Ch 9:2</reference>, “The former inhabitants in their possessions in their cities, were Israel, the priests,” etc., according to which the following words, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference>, “And in Jerusalem there dwelt of the sons of Judah,” etc., can only be understood of the pre-exilic inhabitants. When Bertheau refers, in opposition to this, to <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh 5:15</reference>, where the time between Zerubbabel and Ezra is called the time of the former governors (הראשׁנים הפּחות), with whom Nehemiah contrasts himself, the later governor, to prove that according to that the former inhabitants in our passage may very well denote the inhabitants of the land in the first century of the restored community, he forgets that the governors were changed within short periods, so that Nehemiah might readily call his predecessors in the office “former governors;” while the inhabitants of the cities of Judah, on the contrary, had not changed during the period from Zerubbabel to Ezra, so as to allow of earlier and later inhabitants being distinguished. From the fact that the inhabitants “of their cities” are not contrasted as the earlier, with the inhabitants of Jerusalem as the later, but that both are placed together in such a way as to exclude such a contrast, it is manifest that the conclusion drawn by Movers and Bertheau from <reference osisRef="Neh.11.1">Neh 11:1</reference>, that the “former inhabitants in their possessions in their cities” are those who dwelt in Jerusalem before it was peopled by the inhabitants of the surrounding district, is not tenable. In Neh 11, on the contrary, the register is introduced by the remark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference>, “These are the heads of the province who dwelt in Jerusalem; and they dwelt in the cities of Judah, each in his possession in their cities, Israel, the priests,” etc. This introduction, therefore, announces a register of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and of the other cities of Judah, at that time, i.e., at the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. To this corresponds the manner in which the register has been made out, as in vv. 3-24 the inhabitants of Jerusalem are enumerated, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.25-1Chr.9.36">1Ch 9:25-36</reference> the inhabitants of the other cities. The register in our chapter, on the contrary, deals only with the inhabitants of Jerusalem (vv. 3-19 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), while in vv. 19 <hi type="italic">b</hi>-34 there follow remarks as to the duties devolving upon the Levites. No mention is made in the register of the inhabitants of other cities, or of Israelites, priests, and Levites, who dwelt in their cities outside of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2">1Ch 9:2</reference>), because all that was necessary had been already communicated in the preceding genealogies (1 Chron 2-8).
entries.ce2cb1693e5974a1d894d250912ba89e9b4d5a9a: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference>, too, is not, as Bertheau and others think, “the superscription of the register of those dwelling in Jerusalem;” for were it that, mention must have been made in it of the priests and Levites, the enumeration of whom fills up the greater part of the following register, vv. 10-33. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference> corresponds rather to <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35">1Ch 9:35</reference>, and serves to introduce the contents of the whole chapter, and with it commences the enumeration itself. In Neh 11, consequently, we have a register of the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, while our chapter contains only a register of the former inhabitants of Jerusalem. Only in so far as it treats of the inhabitants of Jerusalem does Nehemiah’s register resemble ours in plan; that is, to this extent, that the sons of Judah, the sons of Benjamin, priests and Levites, are enumerated seriatim as dwelling in Jerusalem, that is, that heads of the fathers'-houses of these inhabitants, as is stated by Nehemiah in the superscription <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:3</reference>, and in our chapter, at the end of the respective paragraphs, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.9">1Ch 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.13">1Ch 9:13</reference>, and in the subscription, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.33">1Ch 9:33</reference> and 1Ch 9:34. <div eID="gen5666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5667" type="x-p"/> But if we examine the contents of the two catalogues more minutely, their agreement is shown by the identity of several of the names of these heads. On this point Bertheau thus speaks: “Of the three heads of Judah, Uthai, Asaiah, and Jeuel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.4-1Chr.9.6">1Ch 9:4-6</reference>, we recognise the first two in Athaiah and Maaseiah, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.4-Neh.11.5">Neh 11:4-5</reference>; only the third name, Jeuel, is omitted. Of the five heads of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.5-1Chr.9.7">1Ch 9:5-7</reference>, it is true, we meet with only two, Sallu and Hodaviah, in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.7-Neh.11.9">Neh 11:7-9</reference>; but it is manifest that there was no intention to communicate in that place a complete enumeration of the hereditary chiefs of Benjamin. The names of the six heads of the divisions of the priests, Jedaiah and Jehoiarib, Jachin, Azariah (Seriah occupies his place in the book of Nehemiah), Adaiah and Maasiai (represented in Nehemiah by Amashai), are enumerated in both places in the same order. Among the Levites there occur the names of Shemaiah and Mattaniah as representatives of the great Levitic divisions of Merari and Gershon-Asaph, and we easily recognise our עבדיה in the עבדּא of the book of Nehemiah. Only the two first of the four chiefs of the doorkeepers, Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, and Ahiman, are named in the abridged enumeration of the book of Nehemiah, while the two others are only referred to in the added ואחיהם.” Now, even according to this statement of the matter, the difference is seen to be almost as great as the agreement; but in reality, as a more exact comparison of the catalogues shows, the true state of the case is very different. According to <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:3</reference>, there dwelt in Jerusalem also sons of Ephraim and Manasseh; but the catalogue from <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.4">1Ch 9:4</reference> onwards contains only sons of Judah and Benjamin, and not a single Ephraimite or Manassite. The reason of that is probably this, that only single families and individuals from among the latter dwelt there, while the register only makes mention of the heads of the larger family groups in the population of Jerusalem.
entries.5a5f2cb3087221857121168fc8597599542c6653: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.4">1Ch 9:4</reference> <div eID="gen5667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5668" type="x-p"/> In the same place there dwelt, of the sons of Judah, three chiefs of the three most important families of Judah, that of Pharez, that of Shelah, and that of Zerah; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.3">1Ch 2:3</reference>-4. Of the family of Pharez was Uthai, whose descent is traced back in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.4">1Ch 9:4</reference> to Bani, of the children of Pharez. The Kethibh בן־בנימן־בּני is clearly to be read according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> מן־בּני בן־בּני. The name Bani occurs, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.31">1Ch 6:31</reference>, among the Merarites; while in the genealogies of Judah, 1 Chron 2-4, neither Bani nor Uthai, nor any one of his ancestors who are here named, is mentioned. In <reference osisRef="Neh.11.4">Neh 11:4</reference>, on the contrary, there is named of the sons of Pharez, Athaiah (עתיה, perhaps only another form of עוּתי), with quite other ancestors; while not a single one of the five names of the persons through whom his race is traced back to Mahalaleel, of the sons of Pharez, coincides with the ancestors of Uthai.
entries.f54bfe326dd96bbe9bd0e94837bd2006890a8d46: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.5">1Ch 9:5</reference> <div eID="gen5668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5669" type="x-p"/> Of the family of Shelah, Asaiah the first-born, and his other) sons. בּנין, after הבּכור, can only be understood of the other sons or descendants. But the epithet give to Asaiah, השּׁילני, is surprising, for it is a formation from שׁילה or שׁילן, and appears to denote a native of Shiloh, a well-known city of Ephraim. This derivation, however, is not suitable, since here the sons (descendants) of Judah are enumerated; and no connection between the inhabitants of Judah and the Ephraimite city Shiloh can either be proved or is at all likely. The older commentators, therefore, have suggested the reading השּׁלני, as in Num 26:20, where the family of Shelah, the third sons of Judah, is so called. This suggestion is doubtless correct, and the erroneous punctuation השּׁילני has probably arisen only from the <hi type="italic">scriptio plena</hi> of the word שׁילה instead of שׁלה. This supposition is confirmed by the fact that the form השּׁלני is found in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.5">Neh 11:5</reference>, although it also is pointed השּׁלני. In Neh. <hi type="italic">loc. cit.</hi>, instead of Asaiah, Maaseiah is introduced as בּן־השּׁלני in the seventh generation, while no ancestors whatever of our Asaiah are mentioned. The name עשׂיה, moreover, is not unfrequent, and occurs in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.36">1Ch 4:36</reference> among the Simeonites; in <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.15">1Ch 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.6">1Ch 15:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.11">1Ch 15:11</reference>, among the Levites; in 2Ki 22:12, 2Ki 22:14 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.20">2Ch 34:20</reference>, as עבד of the King Josiah. מעשׁיה is the name of many persons, e.g., in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference>, and likewise in <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.1">2Ch 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">Jer 29:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.35.4">Jer 35:4</reference>; and elsewhere it is used of men of other tribes: so that even should Maaseiah have been written instead of Asaiah merely by an error of transcription, we are not warranted in identifying our Asaiah with the Maaseiah of Nehemiah.
entries.2f84ac01245693399e2ba6120e10404778c3c030: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.6">1Ch 9:6</reference> “Of the sons of Zerah, Jeuel;” also the name of various persons; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.7">1Ch 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.11">2Ch 26:11</reference> : the register in Neh 11 notices no descendants of Zerah. “And their brethren, 690 (men).” The plural suffix in אחיהם cannot be referred, as Bertheau thinks, to Jeuel, for that name, as being that of the head of a father's-house, cannot be a collective. The suffix most consequently refer to the three heads mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.4-1Chr.9.6">1Ch 9:4-6</reference>, Uthai, Asaiah, and Jeuel, whose brethren are the other heads of fathers'-houses of the three families descended from Judah; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.9">1Ch 9:9</reference>, where the number of the אחים mentioned refers to all the heads who had formerly been spoken of.
entries.156beba8a65d454a7ea26b658caf8cd4b64cabb2: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.7-1Chr.9.9">1Ch 9:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen5669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5670" type="x-p"/> Of the sons of Benjamin, i.e., of the Benjamites, four heads are named, Sallu, Ibneiah, Elah, and Meshullam; and of the first and fourth of these, three generations of ancestors are mentioned, of the second only the father, of the third the father and grandfather. “And their brethren according to their generations, 956;” cf. on 1Ch 9:6. “All these men” are not the brethren whose number is given, but the heads who have been mentioned by name. Now, if we compare this with Neh 11, we meet in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.7-1Chr.9.9">1Ch 9:7-9</reference> with only one of the four heads of Benjamin, Sallu, and that too, as in the Chronicle, as a son of Meshullam, while the ancestors of both are different. Instead of the three others in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.8">1Ch 9:8</reference>, we have סלּי גּבּי, 928; and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.9">1Ch 9:9</reference>, as overseer (prefect), and Jehudah as ruler over the city.
entries.14ba4652c9a626a36c805c39f48106fc3ddcf25b: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10-1Chr.9.13">1Ch 9:10-13</reference> <hi type="italic">The priests.</hi> - The three names Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10">1Ch 9:10</reference>) denote three classes of priests (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.7">1Ch 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.17">1Ch 24:17</reference>), who accordingly dwelt in Jerusalem. There also dwelt there (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.11">1Ch 9:11</reference>) Azariah the son of Hilkiah, etc., the prince of the house of God; cf. 2Ch 31:13. This is the Azariah mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.13">1Ch 6:13</reference>, the son of Hilkiah, etc., the grandfather of the Jehozadak who was led captive into Babylon. then in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.12">1Ch 9:12</reference> we have two other heads of the priestly fathers'-houses, with an enumeration of their ancestors, through whom they are traced back to the classes of priests to which they belonged respectively, viz., Adaiah to the class Malchijah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.9">1Ch 24:9</reference>), and Maasiai to the class Immer (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.14">1Ch 24:14</reference>). According to this, therefore, there dwelt at Jerusalem, of the priesthood, the three classes Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin, Azariah the prince of the temple, and of the classes Malchijah and Immer, the fathers'-houses Adaiah and Maasiai. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.13">1Ch 9:13</reference> the whole number is estimated at 1760. A difficulty is raised by the first words of this verse, “And their brethren, heads of their fathers'-houses, 1760,” which can hardly be taken in any other sense than as denoting that the number of the heads of the fathers'-houses amounted to 1760. This, however, is not conceivable, as “fathers'-houses” are not single households, but larger groups of related families. Moreover, אחיהם, which is co-ordinate with the heads of the fathers'-houses, can only denote, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.6">1Ch 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.9">1Ch 9:9</reference>, the heads of the families which belonged to or constituted the fathers'-houses. To arrive at this meaning, however, we must transpose the words ואחיהם and לבית־אבותם ראשׁים, connecting לבית־אבותם ר with <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.12">1Ch 9:12</reference>, and אחיהם with the number, thus: heads of fathers'-houses, etc., were those mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.12">1Ch 9:12</reference>, and their brethren 1760 (men), valiant heroes in the work of the service of the house of God. Before מלאכת one would expect the word עשׁי, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.24">1Ch 23:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.11.12">Neh 11:12</reference>, but its presence is not so absolutely necessary as to warrant us in supposing that it has been dropped out, and in inserting it. מלאכת may be also taken as an accusative of relation, “valiant heroes in reference to the work;” or at most a ל a tso may be supplied before מלאכת, as it might easily have been omitted by a clerical error after the immediately preceding חיל. On comparing our passage with <reference osisRef="Neh.11.10-Neh.11.14">Neh 11:10-14</reference>, we find there, if בּן־יויריב in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.10">1Ch 9:10</reference> be altered into יהויריב, the same three classes of priests; but instead of Azariah, Seraiah is prince of the house of God, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.11">1Ch 9:11</reference> : thereafter we have 822 brethren, performing the work of the house (of God). Then follows Adaiah of the class Malchijah (as in the Chronicles), but with the addition, “his brethren 242;” and then Amashai of the class Immer, but with other ancestors than those of the Maasiai of the Chronicles, and with the addition, “and their brethren, valiant heroes, 128;” and finally, Zabdiel Ben Hagdolim as overseer (president over them). <div eID="gen5670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5671" type="x-p"/> The sum of the three numbers is 1192, as contrasted with the 1760 of the Chronicle.
entries.c7b8166358b665b140d495ce50e2291ae239e8c5: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.14-1Chr.9.16">1Ch 9:14-16</reference> <hi type="italic">The Levites.</hi> - Of these there dwelt in Jerusalem, Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of, etc., a Merarite; and (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.15">1Ch 9:15</reference>) Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal; and Mattaniah the son of Micah, a descendant of Asaph, and consequently a Gershonite (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.16">1Ch 9:16</reference>); and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, as descendant of Jeduthun, consequently also a Merarite; and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, who dwelt in the villages of the Netophathite, i.e., of the lord or possessor of Netopha, a locality in the neighbourhood of Bethlehem; cf. Neh 7:26. This remark does not refer to Shemaiah, who cannot have dwelt at the same time in Jerusalem and in the village of the Netophathite, but to his grandfather or ancestor Elkanah, who is thereby to be distinguished from the other men who bore this name, which often occurs in the family of Kohath. All these men are, according to the analogy of the other names in our register, and according to the express statement of the superscription, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.34">1Ch 9:34</reference>, to be regarded as heads of Levitic fathers'-houses, and were probably leaders of the music, since those mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.15">1Ch 9:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.16">1Ch 9:16</reference> were descendants of Asaph and Jeduthun, and may therefore with certainty be assumed to have belonged to the Levitic musicians. A confirmation of this supposition is found in the superscription, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.33">1Ch 9:33</reference>, inasmuch as the mention of the singers in the first line goes to show that the enumeration of the Levites began with the singers. If we compare <reference osisRef="Neh.11.15-Neh.11.18">Neh 11:15-18</reference> with our passage, we find that these two, Shemaiah and Mattaniah, are mentioned, and on the whole their forefathers have the same names, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.15">1Ch 9:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference>; but between the two we find Shabbethai and Jozabad of the chief of the Levites set over the external service of the house of God. After Mattaniah, who is chief of the Asaphites there also, mention is made of Bakbukiah as the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, a descendant of Jeduthun (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference>); according to which, even if we identify Bakbakkar with Bakbukiah, and Abda with Obadiah, the Heresh, Galal, and Berechiah of the Chronicles are wanting in Nehemiah, and instead of these three, only Jozabad is mentioned.
entries.217db2c8b873a0943a38dc60b32cbcda743eb0f2: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference> “The doorkeepers, Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum the chief.” The service was so divided among the four just named, that each along with his brethren performed the duty of watching by one of the four sides and chief entrances of the temple (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.24">1Ch 9:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:26</reference>), and these four were consequently heads of those divisions of the Levites to whom was committed the duty of the watch. In <reference osisRef="Neh.11.20">Neh 11:20</reference>, on the contrary, the doorkeepers mentioned are Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren, 172 (men); but the other two chiefs named in the Chronicle are there omitted, while in the Chronicle no number is given. Here the agreement between the two registers ceases. In the Chronicle there follows first of all, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.9.18-1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:18-26</reference></hi>, some remarks on the service of the doorkeepers; and then in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.26-1Chr.9.32">1Ch 9:26-32</reference> the duties of the Levites in general are spoken of; and finally, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.32">1Ch 9:32</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.34">1Ch 9:34</reference> we have subscriptions. In Nehemiah, on the other hand, we find in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.20">1Ch 9:20</reference> the statement that the remaining Israelites, priests, and Levites dwelt in their cities; and after some statements as to the service of the Levites, the enumeration of these cities is introduced. <div eID="gen5671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5672" type="x-p"/> In glancing back over the two catalogues, it is seen that the differences are at least as great as the coincidences. But what conclusions are we to deduce from that fact? Bertheau thinks “from this it is certain that both catalogues cannot have been drawn up independently of each other,” and “that both have been derived from one and the same source, which must have been much more complete, and much richer in names, than our present catalogues; cf. Movers, S. 234.” We, however, judge otherwise. The discrepancies are much too great to allow us to refer them to free handling by epitomizers of some hypothetical more detailed catalogue, or to the negligence of copyists. The coincidence, in so far as it actually exists, does not justify us in accepting such far-fetched suppositions, but may be satisfactorily explained in another way. It consists indeed only in this, that in both registers, (1) sons of Judah and Benjamin, priests and Levites, are enumerated; (2) that in each of these four classes of the inhabitants of Jerusalem some names are identical. The first of these coincidences clearly does not in the least prove that the two catalogues are derived from the same source, and treat of the same time; for the four classes enumerated constituted, both before and after the exile, the population of Jerusalem. But neither does the identity of some of the names prove in the slightest degree the identity of the two catalogues, because the names denote, partly classes of inhabitants, and partly heads of fathers'-houses, i.e., of groups of related households, which did not change with each generation, but sometimes continued to exist for centuries; and because, <hi type="italic">à priori</hi>, we should expect that those who returned from exile would, as far as it was possible, seek out again the dwelling-places of their pre-exilic ancestors; and that consequently after the exile, on the whole, the same families who had dwelt at Jerusalem before it would again take up their abode there. In this way the identity of the names Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin in the two catalogues may be accounted for, as these names do not denote persons, but classes of priests, which existed both before and after the exile. A similar explanation would also apply to the names of the doorkeepers Akkub and Talmon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.19">Neh 11:19</reference>), as not merely the priests, but also the other Levites, were divided for the service according to their fathers'-houses into classes which had permanent names (cf. 1 Chron 25 and 26). Of the other names in our register only the following are identical: of the Benjamites, Sallu the son of Meshullam (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.7">1Ch 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.7">Neh 11:7</reference>); of the priests, Adaiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.12">1Ch 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.12">Neh 11:12</reference>), with almost the same ancestors; and of the Levites, Shemaiah and Mattaniah (1Ch 9:10.; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.15">Neh 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.17">Neh 11:17</reference>). All the other names are different; and even if among the priests Maasiai (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.12">1Ch 9:12</reference>) should be identical with Amashai (<reference osisRef="Neh.11.13">Neh 11:13</reference>), and among the Levites Bakbakkar and Obadiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.16">1Ch 9:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.15">1Ch 9:15</reference>) with Bakbukiah and Abda (<reference osisRef="Neh.11.17">Neh 11:17</reference>), we cannot identify the sons of Judah, Uthai and Azaiah (1Ch 9:4.), with Athaiah and Maaseiah (Neh 11:4.), for their ancestors are quite different. The similarity or even the identity of names, were it in two or three generations, cannot of itself prove the identity of the persons, as we have already seen, in the genealogy of the line of Aaron 1Ch 6:3.), that, e.g., the series Amariah, Ahitub, and Zadok recurs at various times; cf. 1Ch 6:11. and 1Ch 6:12. Everywhere in the genealogical lines the same names very often recur, as it was the custom to give the children the names of their ancestors; cf. Tob. 1:9, Luk 1:59. Win. <hi type="italic">bibl. R. W</hi>. ii. S. 133; Hävern. <hi type="italic">Einl</hi>. ii. 1, S. 179f. But if, on the one hand, the identity of these names in the two catalogues is not at all a valid proof of the identity of the catalogues, and by no means justifies us in identifying similarly-sounding names by supposing errors of transcription, on the other hand we must hold that the register refers to the pre-exilic population of Jerusalem, both because of the wide discrepancies in all points, and in accordance with the introductory statements in 1Ch 9:2. This interpretation is also demanded by the succeeding remarks in reference to the service of the Levites, since they throughout refer to the pre-exilic time.
entries.01876f3e0875a2ca082172ea70368c7bb2f90f03: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.18">1Ch 9:18</reference> <hi type="italic">The duties of the Levites.</hi> - 1Ch 9:18. The first half of this verse, “And until now (is he) in the king’s gate eastward,” must be referred to Shallum (Berth.). To imagine a reference to all the doorkeepers, “until now are they,” does not suit <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.24-1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:24-26</reference>, according to which the doorkeepers kept guard upon all the four sides. The eastern gate of the temple was called the king’s gate, because by this gate the king went in and out to the temple; cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.2">Eze 46:1-2</reference>; Eze 41:3. The remark, “until now is Shallum watcher,” etc., presupposes the existence of the temple at the time of the preparation of this register, and points to the pre-exilic time. Against this Bertheau has raised the objection that the name king’s gate may have been retained even in the post-exilic times for the eastern gate. This must of course be in general admitted, but could only be accepted if it were proved that Shallum lived after the exile. This proof Bertheau obtains by taking the words, “until now is Shallum in the king’s gate,” to mean, “that, according to the ancient arrangement, Shallum, the chief of all the doorkeepers, had still to guard the eastern entrance; according to which Shallum would be the collective designation of the whole series of the chiefs of the doorkeepers who lived from David’s time till after the exile;” but the words cannot be thus interpreted. Such an interpretation cannot be made plausible by identifying the name Shallum with Meshelemiah or Shelemiah, to whose lot it fell in the time of David to be doorkeeper to the eastward (<reference osisRef="1Chr.26.1">1Ch 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.14">1Ch 26:14</reference>); for in doing so, we would overlook the fact that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.21">1Ch 9:21</reference> of our chapter also he bears the name Meshelemiah. The circumstance that both Shallum and Meshelemiah are called Ben-Kore, of the sons of Abiasaph, by no means justifies the identification of these two quite different names; for it is neither necessary nor probable that בּן should here be taken in its narrower sense, and Kore regarded as the immediate father of both. The name קרא is repeated in the family of the east doorkeepers, as we learn from <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.14">2Ch 31:14</reference>, where it is stated that this office was held by a Kore ben Jimna. “These (who are named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference>) are the doorkeepers for the camp of the sons of Levi” (of the Levites), - an antiquated expression, bringing to remembrance the time of Moses, when the Levites, on the journey through the wilderness, were encamped about the tabernacle (Num 3:21.).
entries.cb0bf9f5a57812b3e4d0bd68f0c907a546663b2a: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.19">1Ch 9:19</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.19">1Ch 9:19</reference> gives more exact information as to Shallum’s person and his official position. He, the descendant of Kore, the son (descendant) of Abiasaph, a Korahite, and his brethren according to his father's-house (i.e., called brethren because they, like him, belonged to the father's-house of Korah), were over the work of the service, viz., keepers of the thresholds of the tent, i.e., of the house of God, of the temple, which, according to the ancient custom, was called tent, because God’s house was formerly a tent-the tabernacle. “And his fathers (the ancestors of Shallum) were by the encampment of Jahve, guardians of the entrance.” With these words the author of this register goes back into the ancient time; and we learn that Shallum’s ancestors, of the father's-house of the Korahite Abiasaph, had held the office of guardian of the entrance to the house of God from the time of the conquest of Canaan and the setting up of the tabernacle in Shiloh. The remark in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.20">1Ch 9:20</reference>, that Phinehas the son of Eleazar was prince over them in time past, points to the same period. In the book of Joshua and the older books there is no record of the matter; but since the Korahites were descended through Ishhar from Kohath, and the Kohathites held, according to Num 4:4., the first place among the servants of the holy place, and were responsible for the holiest vessels, we cannot doubt that the statement here rests upon accurate historical tradition. The “encampment of Jahve” is the holy place of the tabernacle, the dwelling of Jahve in the midst of His people. This designation also is derived from the circumstances of the Israelites in their wandering in the Arabian desert, and is likewise employed in <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.2">2Ch 31:2</reference> in reference to Solomon’s temple; but in our verse the tabernacle is intended. It had only one entrance, מבוא, the guarding of which was entrusted to the above-mentioned Korahites.
entries.32956617bdcbe0050c55675294ea6739fdbef058: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.20">1Ch 9:20</reference> <div eID="gen5672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5673" type="x-p"/> Phinehas was prince over them, not as high priest, but during the high-priesthood of his father Eleazar, i.e., in the time of Joshua, just as Eleazar, under the high-priesthood of Aaron in the time of Moses, had the oversight of the keepers of the holy place, as prince of the princes of Levi (Num 3:32). The words עמּו יהוה do not contain a historical remark, “Jahve was with him,” for then the conjunction w would stand before it, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.9">1Ch 11:9</reference>; they are a blessing - “Jahve be with him” - in reference, probably, to the covenant of peace entered into with him and his descendants by Jahve (Num 25:11-13).
entries.ad70144c3a09c4943f55200660f4705cd824e673: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.21">1Ch 9:21</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.21">1Ch 9:21</reference> is quite unconnected with the preceding context, the conjunction w being omitted, and its contents also present considerable difficulties. Zechariah, the son of Meshelemiah, can only be the Zechariah who is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.2">1Ch 26:2</reference> as the first-born of Meshelemiah, and who lived in the time of David; for at the time when David divided the porters into classes, there fell to him the lot towards midnight, i.e., the duty of waiting at the door on the north side of the holy place (<reference osisRef="1Chr.26.14">1Ch 26:14</reference>). With this, indeed, the general statement of our verse, “he was porter of the door (or the entrance) of the tent of the covenant,” is not inconsistent. But what purpose does this general statement serve? With what design is Zechariah, and he alone, mentioned? We have no means of giving a definite answer to this question; but he may perhaps be named as being the person who, before David’s division of the Levites into classes was carried out, had charge of the porters’ service in the tabernacle. But even if this conjecture be accepted as well grounded, the abrupt way in which it is mentioned still remains enigmatical.
entries.3f4b67d394b0696b995b727c1bb9ffdee2c1d128: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">1Ch 9:22</reference> <div eID="gen5673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5674" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">1Ch 9:22</reference> the narrative seems to return to the enumeration begun in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17-1Chr.9.19">1Ch 9:17-19</reference>, so that the reflections on the earlier times, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.19-1Chr.9.21">1Ch 9:19-21</reference>, are to be regarded as a parenthesis. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">1Ch 9:22</reference> runs: “They all who were chosen for doorkeepers for the thresholds, 212 (men): they, in their villages were they registered; they were ordained by David and Samuel the seer on their fidelity.” The infinitive התיחשׂ is used substantively, “in reference to them, in their villages as their genealogical registration accomplished.” If <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">1Ch 9:22</reference> be the continuation of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17-1Chr.9.21">1Ch 9:17-21</reference></hi>, then the number given (212) will refer to the doorkeepers in active service at the time of the preparation of the register. With this hypothesis, however, the last clause of the verse, which states that David and Samuel had appointed them, does not seem to harmonize. But if we consider that the four men mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference> are heads of fathers'-houses, and that their fathers'-houses were not extinguished at the death of their temporary heads, and performed the same service from generation to generation, it might well be said of the generation performing the service at the time of the preparation of our register, that David had appointed them to their office. The case would of course be similar, if, as we have above supposed, the four names in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference> are designations of the classes of doorkeepers, for these classes also performed the same service continually. The statements of our 22nd verse cannot be referred to the time of David, for in <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.8-1Chr.26.10">1Ch 26:8-10</reference> the number of the doorkeepers appointed by David amounted only to eighty, viz., sixty-two of the sons of Obed-Edom, and eighteen of the sons of Meshelemiah, which, with the addition of thirteen Merarites (<reference osisRef="1Chr.26.10-1Chr.26.11">1Ch 26:10-11</reference>), gives a total of ninety-three, while in our verse the number is 212. According to Ezr 2:42, the number of doorkeepers who returned with Zerubbabel was 139 men; and in the register, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.19">Neh 11:19</reference>, the number is stated to be 172. From the remark that they were registered in their villages (חצריהם, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.41">1Ch 6:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.23">Jos 13:23</reference>, and elsewhere), we learn that the doorkeepers dwelt in villages near Jerusalem, whence they came to the city so often as their service required, as the singers also did in the post-exilic time, Neh 12:29. יסּד, to found, set, ordain, and so appoint to an office. “David and Samuel the seer:” הראה, the ancient designation of the prophets, for which at a later time נביא was the more usual word; cf. 1Sa 9:9. Nowhere else do we find any record of Samuel’s having taken any part in David’s arrangement of the service of the Levites in the holy place. Samuel, moreover, was no longer living when David began to arrange the worship at the time when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, for he died before Saul, and consequently before the beginning of David’s reign; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">1Sa 25:1</reference> with 1Sa 28:3. Bertheau is consequently of opinion that this statement of our historian rests merely upon the general recollection, according to which the worship was organized afresh, and established in its newer form, in the time of David and Samuel. This is of course possible, but there is no cogent reason against accepting the much less remote supposition that the chronicler took this remark from his authority. The mention of Samuel after David has not a chronological signification, but David is named first on account of his connection with the matter in hand; for the thorough re-organization of the worship, and the classification of the persons engaged in carrying it on, originated with David. For these arrangements of David, however, Samuel had prepared the way in his struggle for the restoration of the theocracy, and of the worship which had fallen into desuetude under Eli and his profligate sons. To do this in any measure, he must have, without doubt, ordained trustworthy men to the individual offices, and thus have prepared the way for King David. בּאמוּנתם is found in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.31">1Ch 9:31</reference> without the suffix, with the meaning “in good faith” (cf. 2Ki 12:16; 2Ki 22:7; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.12">2Ch 31:12</reference>), and accordingly is here upon their fidelity, i.e., because they had been recognised to be faithful.
entries.c20f9f4196325ac88244137bb8d79f82b20aaf7f: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.23-1Chr.9.24">1Ch 9:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen5674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5675" type="x-p"/> They (those ordained by David) and their sons (descendants) were at the doors of the house of Jahve-of the tent-house (האהל בּית is added to בּית־יהוה, in order that the latter might not be confined to Solomon’s temple); for the watch (משׁמרות of persons, as in <reference osisRef="Neh.12.9">Neh 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.4.3">Neh 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.16">Neh 4:16</reference>), according to the four winds (quarters) were they, i.e., the doorkeepers stood so, in accordance with the arrangement made by David; cf. 1Ch 26:14.
entries.51fcd3cf34d34a4f9ea492ab72f5193dd599c5ad: <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.25-1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:25-26</reference> “And their brethren in their villages (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.22">1Ch 9:22</reference>) were bound to come the seventh day, from time to time, with these.” The infinitive בּוא with ל expresses duty, as in 1Ch 5:1. The seventh day is the Sabbath of the week, on which each class in order had to take charge of the services. אלּה עם are the chiefs mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17">1Ch 9:17</reference> who dwelt in Jerusalem, and of whom it is said in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:26</reference>, “for they are on their fidelity, the four mighty of the doorkeepers.” In explanation of the גּבּרי, Bertheau very fittingly compares σταρτηγοῖ τοῦ Ἱεροῦ, Luk 22:52. The words הלויּם הם, which may be translated, “they are the Levites,” or “they (viz., the Levites),” are somewhat surprising.
